input: Turning to the resourcing position, it should be noted that a staffing gap of 7 weeks has now opened up within the delivery team. This gap has arisen because members of staff have moved on from the project before their replacements have been able to start, which has unfortunately left a period during which key roles are not covered. The work that is affected sits within the EPC workstream, and the gap is expected to have an impact on the pace at which deliverables can be progressed during the affected period, since the tasks that the departing staff were responsible for cannot simply be picked up by others who are already fully committed to their own work. In order to address this issue, it is proposed that agency cover be approved in order to bridge the gap until the permanent replacements are in place, and it is further proposed that the project manager should own the delivery of this mitigation, including arranging the cover and reassigning the affected work in the meantime. It is hoped that this approach will help to minimise the disruption that might otherwise be caused, although it should be acknowledged that the effectiveness of agency cover will depend to a considerable extent on how quickly suitable individuals can be identified and brought on board, and on how much handover can be achieved in the circumstances. The full extent of the gap is 7 weeks, and the matter is raised here so that it can be considered alongside the other resourcing pressures that the team is currently facing, with a view to reaching a position that protects the programme as far as reasonably possible.
target: A staffing gap of 7 weeks stands in the delivery team. Staff have left the project before their replacements start, and the roles they held are uncovered for that period. The uncovered work sits inside the EPC scope, and it does not redistribute itself: the remaining staff are committed to their own deliverables, and the tasks attached to the vacant roles wait for cover or for the replacements. Deliverables that depend on those tasks move with them. The mitigation proposed is agency cover for the gap, approved by the project board, with the project manager owning its delivery: engaging the cover, settling the incoming staff into the vacant roles, and reassigning the affected work until the cover is in place. Agency cover shortens the gap only where the vacant roles can be filled from the agency market at the specialisms the project needs, and cover engaged late shortens it by less than its full length. The 7 weeks therefore remains the planning figure until cover is actually in post, and any programme commitment made in the meantime should be read against the uncovered figure rather than against the mitigated one. The board is asked to treat the gap as a schedule risk on that basis: a period in which named work has no owner, with a mitigation whose effect is real only once the people are in place. The cause is structural rather than personal: recruitment runs behind departure on this project, and a leaver's notice period ends before a successor can be selected, cleared, and started. Until that sequence shortens, any departure in a scarce specialism opens a gap of the same kind, and the cover proposed here treats the present instance rather than the pattern. The board may therefore want the recruitment position itself reported alongside the gap, so that the next gap is forecast rather than discovered.
